Microsoft Planetary Computer is a cloud-based platform that combines global environmental data with computational tools to enable geospatial analysis, sustainability insights, and AI-driven environmental decision-making.
roboto
Overview
The Microsoft Planetary Computer is designed to support environmental sustainability and conservation efforts by providing access to a multi-petabyte catalog of global geospatial and environmental data in analysis-ready formats, accessible via APIs and Azure Storage

roboto
roboto
HYPERLINK "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/"Microsoft+1. It allows scientists, researchers, policymakers, and developers to measure, monitor, and model ecosystems, helping to answer complex questions about the Earth
s environment

Comparison with Other Platforms

HYPERLINK "https://mapscaping.com/microsofts-planetary-computer-vs-google-earth-engine-a-compare-and-contrast/"mapscaping.com. This makes it particularly suitable for organizations that need to combine geospatial data with AI and enterprise analytics.

Calibri
Physical climate risk data and analytics to assess, price and report climate exposure on assets and portfolios.
Calibri
Alpha-Klima is the climate-risk unit of Arfima Financial Services, based in Madrid. Our platform links climate hazard data to asset-level impacts and then to financial and regulatory metrics, built on OS-Climate's open-source physrisk library, where we are active contributors along with BNP Paribas. See 
HYPERLINK "https://alpha-klima.com/"https://alpha-klima.com for more information.
1111
Calibri
Calibri
Datasets on offer:
Hazard indicators for flood, heat, wildfire, wind, hail and snow, drought, water stress, landslide, subsidence and earthquake, under historical and future climate scenarios to 2050-2085, together with asset impact, and portfolio loss metrics. Synthetic example portfolios are included to get started.

Who and what:
Can We Finance Regeneration Without Extracting From Communities
Segoe UI
Segoe UI
How do we use our resources together to achieve our visions?
Segoe UI
Communities often have real capacity in the form of people, skills, spaces, relationships, local demand, future production, food, land, care, trust and shared purpose. But this capacity is often fragmented across plans, spreadsheets, conversations, grant reports, bank records and informal networks. The challenge is to build tools that help communities see what they have, define what they need, make credible commitments, route support, and track fulfilment.
In that framing:
One Planet can help map plans, actors, places, outcomes, actions and indicators.
Sarafu can help map offers, requests, redeemable commitments, pools, limits, exchanges, fulfilment histories and settlement flows.
Together, this gives hackers a way to move from static plans to actionable coordination.
For the four live problem statements, I would frame Sarafu
s role like this:
1. Collaboration Reverse Challenge
One Planet can map the plans, stakeholders, places, outcomes and possible conflicts. Sarafu can help express who is committing what, under what conditions, and whether those commitments are fulfilled. This turns coordination from a planning exercise into a delivery and accountability layer.
2. From Underbanked to Understood (Community Credit and Commitment Pools)
This is the most direct fit for Sarafu. The platform can help make community capacity visible through commitment pools, voucher flows, participation records, redemption, fulfilment and settlement histories. This can help banks, councils and funders understand community reliability and investability through richer evidence than cash flow alone.
3. From Satellite to Community Space
Geospatial and satellite data can identify risks such as flooding, drought, pollution or land-use pressure. Sarafu can help communities coordinate the response: local labour, materials, food, transport, repairs, stewardship, mutual support and follow-up commitments.
4. Resolving Food and Energy Insecurity
Sarafu can help coordinate producers, households, schools, hospitals, councils, community hubs and local businesses through offers, requests, procurement commitments, demand signals, local food flows and fulfilment records. This could support work on reducing the healthy food penalty, improving logistics and linking local producers with community demand.
A curated published dataset or anonymised sample dataset. (latest 
HYPERLINK "https://zenodo.org/records/20120190"https://zenodo.org/records/20120190 )

Logical architecture diagrams visually represent system components, their interactions, and relationships without specifying technology or physical deployment.
roboto
IT Infrastructure Logical Diagram
This type maps software, hardware, and network components, showing how they interact within an organization. It highlights dependencies and relationships between systems, helping plan, deploy, and manage IT resources efficiently. Components often include servers, databases, applications, and network devices, arranged to show logical connections rather than physical placement (Creately) 
roboto
roboto
Calibri
Calibri
HYPERLINK "https://creately.com/diagram/example/ilx6bww31/logical-architecture-diagram"Creately+1.
roboto
Calibri
Presentation Layer: User interfaces and client applications
Calibri
Business Logic Layer: Core processing and rules
Calibri
Data Access Layer: Interaction with databases or external services
Calibri
External Systems: APIs, third-party services, or integrations
Dependencies and communication protocols are clearly represented to guide design and ensure scalability (Tpoint Tech) 
1111
Calibri
HYPERLINK "https://www.tpointtech.com/logical-architecture-diagram"tpointtech.com.
Software System Logical Architecture
Used in software development, these diagrams illustrate high-level organization and relationships between modules, layers, and interfaces. Typical layers include:
Calibri
Calibri
Client Tier: Applications used by end-users
Calibri
Access Tier: Secure communication between client and system
Calibri
Presentation Tier: Interfaces delivering results to users
Calibri
Business Service Tier: Backend processing and logic
Components are often arranged horizontally to represent logical tiers, providing clarity on system operations without specifying technology (EDUCBA) 
1111
Calibri
HYPERLINK "https://www.educba.com/logical-architecture/"EDUCBA.
Logical Component Diagram
Focuses on the abstraction of physical components, showing how logical components interact to fulfill system functionality. Examples include:
Calibri
Logical Functions Breakdown Diagram (LFBD)
Common in model-based systems engineering (MBSE), this diagram refines system functions into logical functions, grouping related functions such as monitoring or control. It helps ensure all system capabilities are represented and linked to logical actors, supporting traceability and design consistency (iExcelArc) 
Calibri
Calibri
HYPERLINK "https://iexcelarc.com/logical-architecture/"iexcelarc.com.
Key Examples
Abstraction and Simplification: Focus on key components and interactions, avoiding unnecessary details.
Calibri
Calibri
Standardization: Use consistent symbols, colors, and layout conventions for clarity.
Calibri
Layering: Organize components into logical tiers or layers to show functional separation.
Calibri
Interfaces and Dependencies: Clearly indicate communication paths and dependencies between components.
Calibri
External Integrations: Highlight connections to external systems, APIs, or services to show interdependencies.
These examples provide a foundation for creating logical architecture diagrams that are clear, scalable, and useful for communication among developers, architects, and stakeholders.
1111

Build around a single, painful transaction and grow both sides together.

Once enough communities are doing this, liquidity naturally becomes the next problem.

Rather than treating conferences as marketing, treat them as onboarding.
Phase 5
Phase 4
Phase 3
Phase 2
Don't Build a Marketplace
One of the biggest lessons from marketplace history is that almost nobody successfully builds supply first and demand later.
Calibri
Calibri
The graveyard is full of marketplaces that spent years building inventory and then discovered no one was transacting.
Likewise, building demand first often creates disappointment because there is nothing useful available.
The real answer is usually:
Segoe UI
Airbnb didn't start with "global accommodation supply."
Uber didn't start with "millions of riders."
LinkedIn didn't start with a complete professional network.
They all began with a very small, highly valuable interaction.
For your community liquidity marketplace, the challenge is even harder because you're not creating a marketplace for one asset class. You're creating a marketplace for multiple forms of capital.
That means you need a different growth strategy.
Build a Community Operating System
This sounds counterintuitive.
A marketplace only becomes valuable once enough people participate.
But a tool can be valuable with a single user.
The first question should therefore be:
What can a community do on day one that creates value even if nobody else has joined?
Create a digital asset register
Calibri
Calibri
Map community assets
Calibri
Record stewardship activity
Calibri
Identify underutilised land
Calibri
Track social impact
Calibri
Catalogue local skills
For example:
If one community council or CLT gets value immediately, you have something deployable.
The marketplace emerges later.

Calibri

must happen simultaneously.

Calibri

is often the real sequence.
Many communities don't even know what assets exist locally.
What assets do we have?

Imagine the first version simply answers:
That's useful before a marketplace exists.

One town

The objective is not scale.
The objective is proving:
liquidity can be created where none previously existed.
Once proven locally, replication becomes easier.

Create Demand Before Calling It Demand
One thing I've noticed from your SF.Live and community wealth work:
You already have demand.
It just doesn't look like marketplace demand.

Think Like LinkedIn
LinkedIn didn't begin as a recruitment marketplace.
It began as a professional identity network.
Recruitment emerged later.

The Critical Insight
I suspect the winning strategy is not:
It is:
At that point the marketplace is no longer a speculative idea. It becomes the obvious infrastructure layer connecting communities, investors, stewardship providers and local assets.
In other words, the first product may not actually be a marketplace at all. It may be a community wealth discovery and stewardship platform, with the marketplace emerging as the second act. That approach dramatically reduces the chicken-and-egg problem and is probably the lowest-cost route to adoption and scale.

Marketplace of Marketplaces.
The architecture is probably much simpler than most people initially imagine.
Segoe UI
The mistake many marketplace builders make is to think they need to build a giant marketplace database first. Five years ago that was largely true. Today, with vector search, RAG, knowledge graphs, agents and MCP-style connectors, you can federate existing marketplaces rather than replace them.
Segoe UI
Level 1: The Existing Ecosystem
Grant marketplaces
Calibri
Calibri
Innovation challenge platforms
Calibri
Community finance providers
Calibri
Impact investment platforms
Calibri
Crowdfunding sites
Calibri
Carbon marketplaces
Calibri
Nature credit platforms
Calibri
Community Land Trust projects
Calibri
Local authority opportunities
Calibri
Corporate sustainability programmes
Calibri
Accelerator programmes
Calibri
OnePlanet and similar graph systems
You already have:
opportunities
Calibri
Calibri
applications
Calibri
funding
Calibri
organisations
Calibri
projects
Calibri
places
Calibri
outcomes
Most of these already contain:
The problem is they all describe these differently.
Level 2: A Common Ontology
This is the critical piece.
Instead of integrating systems technically, integrate them conceptually.
Everything becomes one of:
Actor
Person
Organisation
Community
Resource
Money
Land
Buildings
Skills
Data
Technology
Opportunity
Grant
Tender
Project
Hackathon
Challenge
Outcome
Carbon
Nature
Employment
Wellbeing
Resilience
Location
Place
Region
Catchment
Community
Consolas
This is essentially what OnePlanet is doing with graph concepts.
Underneath, every marketplace keeps its own database.
You only map their concepts to your ontology.
Level 3: Knowledge Graph
You then create a graph:
Tesco
  provides
Community Grant
Community Grant
  funds
Community Garden
Community Garden
  improves
Biodiversity
Biodiversity
  contributes_to
Nature Recovery
Nature Recovery
  supports
Surrey Nature Strategy
The graph starts to connect previously disconnected marketplaces.
This is where the magic begins.
Level 4: Marketplace Connectors
Each marketplace gets a connector.
These can be:
Easy
Website scraping
Better
APIs
Best
MCP servers
(MCP = Model Context Protocol)
Increasingly marketplaces will expose MCP endpoints designed for AI agents.
Your system doesn't have to own the data.
It simply indexes and understands it.
Level 5: RAG Layer
This is where things have changed dramatically in the last two years.
Traditionally you would need:
Marketplace A schema
Marketplace B schema
Marketplace C schema
and then manually harmonise them.
Now:
Marketplace A
     |
Marketplace B
     |-----> Embeddings
Marketplace C
All content gets vectorised.
The AI can understand that:
community resilience fund
place-based adaptation grant
may be conceptually similar.
RAG does not replace ontology.
But it makes mapping far easier.
Think:
Ontology = structure
RAG = understanding
You need both.
Level 6: Agent Layer
This is where the user experience changes.
Instead of:
Search
Browse
Apply
The user says:
"I'm a village hall in Surrey looking for 
50k to add solar panels and improve biodiversity."
Searches all marketplaces
Calibri
Calibri
Finds grants
Calibri
Finds local authority schemes
Calibri
Finds community lenders
Calibri
Finds volunteers
Calibri
Finds suppliers
Calibri
Creates a shortlist
Calibri
Helps complete applications
The agent:
Potentially:
Opportunity Agent
Funding Agent
Nature Agent
Community Agent
Skills Agent
Volunteer Agent
working together.
Level 7: Marketplace Orchestrator
This is the part most people miss.
The future isn't one AI.
It's many specialist agents.
Imagine:
User
   |
Marketplace Concierge
   |
-------------------------
|      |      |      |
Funding Nature Skills Data
Agent   Agent Agent Agent
Each specialises.
The Concierge combines results.
This is exactly where agentic architectures are heading.
Why I Think SustainableFinance.Live Could Be Different
Most marketplaces answer:
"What opportunities exist?"
I think your opportunity is answering:
"What combination of opportunities will achieve my goal?"
For example:
High street grants
Calibri
Calibri
Community bonds
Calibri
Vacant property schemes
Calibri
Biodiversity finance
Calibri
Volunteer groups
Calibri
Local businesses
Calibri
Planning support
Calibri
University partners
The system could discover:
No single marketplace has all of these.
A graph-plus-agent architecture can.
The Architecture I Would Build in 2026
                   USER
                     |
              AI CONCIERGE
                     |
          ---------------------
          |         |        |
      Funding   Community  Nature
       Agent      Agent    Agent
          |         |        |
          -------------------
                    |
             KNOWLEDGE GRAPH
                    |
         -----------------------
         |         |          |
      VECTOR     ONTOLOGY   RAG
       INDEX                 INDEX
         |         |          |
   ------------------------------
   |      |      |      |      |
 Platforms APIs   Portals etc.
My strong view is that you do not want to build "an LLM of all the marketplaces".
Build a shared ontology.
Calibri
Calibri
Build a graph.
Calibri
Use RAG to connect disparate content.
Calibri
Put a multi-agent conversational layer on top.
Instead:
The LLM becomes the interface, not the database.
That's a much cheaper, faster, and more future-proof architecture than trying to consolidate every marketplace into one giant platform. In many ways it's very close to the original vision you described months ago around community liquidity: connecting opportunities, assets, finance, skills, land, projects, and outcomes into a single discoverable ecosystem rather than creating yet another isolated marketplace.
A market place of marketplaces
A market place of marketplaces

Idea Starter 
Credit and Commitment Pools 
. The Sarafu Network enables communities to issue 
Community organisations - such as sports clubs, 
redeemable vouchers for goods, services, and 
charities, housing groups, and local producers - hold 
labour, creating transparent and auditable 
real value through relationships, skills, and local demand. 
commitment pools. 
However, traditional financial systems often see them as 
low value or high risk because of their fragmented 
 Could you build on Sarafu, or design a compatible 
records, limited collateral, and volatile cash flow. 
solution, to help communities coordinate resources, 
route support, and make local capacity visible? 
How might we make these assets, commitments, and 
. Could this data also help banks, councils, and 
histories visible to support fair finance, mutual credit, and 
investors identify which projects are resilient, 
better coordination? 
trustworthy, and investable? 
Can we build tools that help banks and funders 
understand place-based organisations, while enabling 
communities and meet local needs without relying 
solely on cash?

Microsoft Planetary computer
The Microsoft Planetary Computer is designed to support environmental sustainability and conservation efforts by providing access to a multi-petabyte catalog of global geospatial and environmental data in analysis-ready formats, accessible via APIs and Azure Storage 
HYPERLINK "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/"Microsoft+1. It allows scientists, researchers, policymakers, and developers to measure, monitor, and model ecosystems, helping to answer complex questions about the Earth
s environment 
1111111111
The Microsoft Planetary Computer is designed to support environmental sustainability and conservation efforts by providing access to a multi-petabyte catalog of global geospatial and environmental data in analysis-ready formats, accessible via APIs and Azure Storage 
HYPERLINK "https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/"Microsoft+1. It allows scientists, researchers, policymakers, and developers to measure, monitor, and model ecosystems, helping to answer complex questions about the Earth
s environment 
HYPERLINK "https://devblogs.microsoft.com/premier-developer/the-microsoft-planetary-computer/"Microsoft+1. The platform emphasizes open standards and interoperability, using Python-based tools like xarray, rasterio, geopandas, and the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) standard for data cataloging 
11111111111111111

. The business model canvas illustrates the fundamental building blocks of a business, providing a high-level, comprehensive view of the various strategic details required to 
successfully bring a product to market and how the business creates, delivers and captures value. 
. Example template below explains the nine key canvass segments which ideally should be viewed from right (Customer Segments) to left (Key Partners)
